subtopic: Electromagnetic induction (Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law)
notes: Drafted from the wrong options in Induction Lab v1. Add literature references and classroom evidence to each entry before using this for research claims.

misconceptions.label: No battery, no current
misconceptions.learner_says: There is no battery in the circuit, so no current can flow.
misconceptions.correct_idea: A changing magnetic flux through a coil induces an EMF, and that EMF drives a current in a closed circuit. A battery is only one source of EMF.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: Every circuit they have built before had a cell. They link current to the battery instead of to an EMF.
misconceptions.remediation: Do the Observe step with no cell anywhere on screen, then ask: where did the energy come from? (The work done pushing the magnet.)

misconceptions.label: Flux, not change in flux
misconceptions.learner_says: The stronger the field inside the coil, the bigger the EMF, even if nothing moves.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The induced EMF depends on the rate of change of flux linkage (ε = −NΔΦ/Δt). A large but constant flux induces no EMF.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: They mix up 'how much' with 'how fast it changes'. Everyday language rarely tells the two apart.
misconceptions.remediation: Trial 3 (magnet held still): the flux readout is high while the EMF reads zero. Put both numbers side by side and ask the learner to explain the gap.

misconceptions.label: EMF builds up over time
misconceptions.learner_says: The longer the magnet stays in the coil, the further the needle swings.
misconceptions.correct_idea: EMF is not stored or accumulated. It exists only while the flux is changing and drops to zero as soon as the change stops.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: They treat EMF like charge filling a container, or like heating, which does build up over time.
misconceptions.remediation: Hold the magnet still for several seconds and watch the meter stay at zero.

misconceptions.label: Induced current helps the change
misconceptions.learner_says: The coil becomes a south pole and pulls the magnet in.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Lenz's Law: the induced current creates a field that opposes the change in flux. An approaching north pole is met by a north pole.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: They apply 'opposites attract' without thinking about energy. If the coil helped the magnet, energy would come from nowhere.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask: if the coil pulled the magnet in, would it then speed up by itself forever? Use energy conservation to rule it out.

misconceptions.label: A coil cannot have poles
misconceptions.learner_says: Only magnets have poles. A coil of wire cannot have a north or south pole.
misconceptions.correct_idea: A current-carrying coil produces a magnetic field like a bar magnet, with a north and south face given by the right-hand rule.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: They have not linked the Grade 10 'magnetic field around a current' work to coils.
misconceptions.remediation: Revisit the right-hand rule for a solenoid before Lenz's Law.

misconceptions.label: Speed does not matter
misconceptions.learner_says: Pushing the magnet slowly or quickly gives the same EMF.
misconceptions.correct_idea: A faster movement changes the flux in a shorter Δt, so the EMF is larger.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: They focus on the total change in flux, which is the same in both cases, and ignore the time taken.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare the 'Largest EMF' column for trials 1 and 2 in the trial table.
misconceptions.probe_gap: No item in v1 probes this directly. Add a prediction question about slow versus fast.

misconceptions.label: Current only flows one way
misconceptions.learner_says: The needle swings to one side only.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Increasing flux (magnet entering) and decreasing flux (magnet leaving) induce EMFs in opposite directions, so the needle reverses.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: They picture one event ('the magnet goes through') rather than two changes with opposite signs.
misconceptions.remediation: Use the EMF-against-time graph in the Explain step and point to where it changes sign.

misconceptions.label: Leaves out the number of turns
misconceptions.correct_idea: Each turn has an EMF induced in it, so the total is N times larger: ε = NΔΦ/Δt.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: They remember the formula as 'change in flux over time' and drop N.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the learner to say in words what each symbol stands for before substituting.

misconceptions.label: Uses time the wrong way round in a rate
misconceptions.learner_says: ε = N × ΔΦ × Δt, or ΔΦ = ε / (N × Δt)
misconceptions.correct_idea: EMF is a rate: ε = NΔΦ/Δt. Rearranged, ΔΦ = εΔt/N. Time divides the change in ε, so it multiplies when solving for ΔΦ.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: Weak link between 'rate' and division. Same root as EMI-02.
misconceptions.remediation: Connect to speed = distance / time: any 'rate' divides by time.

misconceptions.label: Powers of ten mishandled
misconceptions.learner_says: 3,6 × 10⁻³ is entered as 3,6 × 10³, or the exponent is dropped.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Scientific notation must be entered exactly. Estimating the answer first catches slips of 10⁶.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: Calculator entry errors and weak scientific notation skills, not physics.
misconceptions.remediation: Practise using the EXP or ×10ˣ key, and estimating the order of magnitude before calculating.

misconceptions.label: Gives the magnitude as negative
misconceptions.learner_says: ε = −6,0 V (when the question asks for magnitude)
misconceptions.correct_idea: The minus sign in Faraday's Law shows direction (Lenz's Law). A magnitude is always positive.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: They copy the sign from the formula without knowing what it means.
misconceptions.remediation: Link the minus sign to the Lenz's Law question so it carries meaning.

misconceptions.label: Angle measured from the wrong line
misconceptions.learner_says: The coil is 'placed perpendicularly' in the field, so θ = 90°.
misconceptions.correct_idea: θ is the angle between the magnetic field and the normal to the coil's surface. A field perpendicular to the coil gives θ = 0° and the largest flux.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: The angle shown on a sketch is often the one with the coil itself, and learners use it without checking.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the learner to draw the normal on the sketch before substituting, and check: field along the normal means maximum flux.
misconceptions.status: Confirmed in DBE Grade 11 Physical Sciences P1, November 2018, Question 11 and its marking guidelines.

misconceptions.label: Area not converted to square metres
misconceptions.learner_says: A 3 cm square coil has A = 0,03 m², or A = 9 cm² = 0,09 m².
misconceptions.correct_idea: Square the side and convert: (0,03 m)² = 9 × 10⁻⁴ m². 1 m² = 10⁴ cm², so an area converts with the square of the length factor.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: Converting an area like a length (÷100 instead of ÷10 000), or not converting at all.
misconceptions.remediation: Draw 1 m² as a 100 cm × 100 cm square to show why the factor is 10 000.
misconceptions.status: Confirmed in DBE Grade 11 Physical Sciences P1, November 2018, Question 11 and its marking guidelines.

misconceptions.label: Right-hand rule misapplied to a solenoid
misconceptions.learner_says: Picks the current direction from the induced pole using the wrong hand or with fingers and thumb swapped.
misconceptions.correct_idea: For a solenoid, curl the fingers of the right hand in the direction of the current. The thumb points to the north pole.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: Several hand rules are taught in Grade 10 and 11, and learners mix them up.
misconceptions.remediation: After using Lenz's Law to find the induced pole, apply the solenoid rule as a separate, named second step.
misconceptions.status: Confirmed in DBE Grade 11 Physical Sciences P1, November 2018, Question 11 and its marking guidelines.

misconceptions.label: Final flux taken as the change in flux
misconceptions.correct_idea: ΔΦ = Φ_final − Φ_initial = BA(cos θ_f − cos θ_i). A coil that starts facing the field already has flux BA through it.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: They read Δ as 'the flux at the end', the same root as confusing flux with change in flux (EMI-02).
misconceptions.remediation: Before substituting, ask for Φ at the start and Φ at the end as two separate numbers, then subtract.
misconceptions.status: Confirmed in DBE Grade 11 Physical Sciences P1, November 2018, Question 11 and its marking guidelines.

misconceptions.label: Confuses Faraday's Law with Lenz's Law
misconceptions.learner_says: Faraday's Law: the induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change that caused it.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Faraday's Law gives the size of the induced emf (proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage). Lenz's Law gives its direction (opposing the change).
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: The two laws are taught together for the same experiment, and both are 'the induction law' in learners' notes.
misconceptions.remediation: Teach them as a pair with one question each: Faraday answers 'how big?', Lenz answers 'which way?'.
misconceptions.status: Draft: found while building the constructed challenge set (evaluation/challenge_set.csv). Needs classroom or literature evidence.

misconceptions.label: Moving faster makes the magnet stronger
misconceptions.learner_says: The emf increases because the magnetic field becomes stronger when the coil rotates (or the magnet moves) faster.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The field strength B stays the same. Moving faster makes the same change in flux happen in less time, so the rate of change of flux, and the emf, increase.
misconceptions.why_learners_think_this: They need a cause for the bigger emf and attach it to the most visible quantity, the magnet's strength.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what the magnet is made of and whether that changed. Then compare ΔΦ and Δt for slow and fast movements.

item_map.text: Nothing. There is no battery in the circuit, so no current can flow.
It swings to one side and stays there while the magnet is inside.
It swings one way, then swings back the other way.
It swings further the longer the magnet stays in the coil.
A large reading, because the field inside the coil is strong.
A small reading, because some field still passes through the coil.
A south pole, because opposite poles attract and the coil pulls the magnet in.
A north pole, because the induced current opposes the approaching magnet.
Neither, because a coil cannot have magnetic poles.

text_items.question: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed into a solenoid. X is the end of the solenoid facing the magnet; A and B are the ends of the wire. (The sketch shows the winding direction.) Which pole will be induced at point X? Write only NORTH or SOUTH. (1)

The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed into a solenoid. X is the end of the solenoid facing the magnet; A and B are the ends of the wire. (The sketch shows the winding direction.) In which direction will the induced current flow? Write only FROM A TO B or FROM B TO A. (1)
text_items.notes: The marker cannot see the winding in this text; the memo answer is FROM A TO B.
